title: Human Drivers Are A Public Health Menace (And One Tried to Kill Me Recently!)
subtitle: Or, "is this the most compelling case for AI my daughter Quinn has ever seen?"
body_html:
Self-Driving cars are the first experience with fully autonomous robots that feel like real, actual magic. I’m speaking only of Waymo—not my former Tesla. I have taken a Waymo in Phoenix, but in the chaos of San Fransisco, the magic really hits you.

You know what else really hit me? A human driver.

Don't worry, Quinn is interviewed at the end of this article.

Traffic accidents are a real menace, I’d be remiss if I didn’t add. I was hit in a hit and run, in which I was injured, but my daughter was not, this April. I was rear-ended, and then the car was rammed again by the driver to get away from the scene. The police later arrested the gentleman. I have suspicions that he was drunk, but I will leave that to the authorities.

It was quite unsettling.

I survived. My daughter, Quinn, was buckled in the backseat. Thanks, seatbelts. Others in my life have not been so lucky. One of my favorite people, ever, Katie Fisher, was killed by a reckless driver, at the age of 24. Her brother was a dear friend for many years. Her family was never the same—how could they be?

Oh, it also turned into a legal hell!

Her brother, Matt, wrote about what happened:

I’ll try to cleave to the facts. On June 19, 2010, my sister was driving in Baltimore when her car was struck by another car and she was killed. The other driver had run a red light and hit my sister as she crossed the intersection on the green light.

The insurance company event called witnesses against the now-decreased Katie, so as to avoid paying out on an insurance policy.

The killer’s policy settled, usually what happens when the party is at fault:

One indication that the case was pretty open-and-shut was that the other guy’s insurance company looked at the situation and settled with my sister’s estate basically immediately. Now, because the other driver was underinsured, that payment didn’t amount to much, but my sister carried a policy with Progressive against the possibility of an accident with an underinsured driver. So Progressive was now on the hook for the difference between the other guy’s insurance and the value of Katie’s policy.

Progressive chose to mount a strong case against the estate of their policy holder and defend the man who negligently killed her.

To quote Matt’s conclusion about what a at the time, on his blog:

"someday when you have your accident, I promise that there will be enough wiggle room for Progressive's bottomless stack of in-house attorneys to make a court case out of it and to hammer at that court case until you or your surviving loved ones run out of money."

These are the kind of deaths that strike from the depths of hell and seem so senseless.

On top of that, victims and their families have to content with corporate bad behavior. I was thrilled to be alive for my call with Hertz, from whom I had rented my car due to supply chain issues with my car’s repair in process. I had one call where they told me not to drive my car—which had just been hit—all the was home. Then, in the follow up, they told me it should be fine…at which point I started recording, because being lied to right after someone tries to kill me and my kid is a best time to start with a gifted provocateur such as your author.

Owen: Just recording this for posterity’s sake.

Patty: We do request that you do not record calls. If the call is recorded we will have to disconnect.

Owen: You are misreporting what was previously said to me on prior calls, and I want to make sure I have an accurate record of what we say.

Patty: At this point we will have to disconnect the call if you’re recording.

Owen: If you’re going to do that, this is not going to go well. How could you even know? What if I were recording you on another device and you didn’t know? I am making it clear and letting you know.

Patty: I heard it, and unfortunately we are not allowed to be recorded. We will have to disconnect the call.

Owen: I will escalate to your manager immediately.

Patty: Give me just a moment. Hold on for me.

Owen: To be super clear, in Connecticut, your recording notice at the beginning of the call saying “this call may be recorded” serves as obtaining consent from both parties.

Patty: No sir, that lets you know that we are recording the call to make sure we are giving you the correct information.

Owen: That is two-party consent under Connecticut law. Where are you physically located?

Patty: I am in Texas.

Owen: I am physically in the state of Connecticut, where that warning at the beginning of the call counts as two-party consent. We both agreed at the beginning of the call to have it recorded. Your corporate policy is not a legal policy and does not supersede our contract between the two parties. Please escalate me to a supervisor.

Patty: With Hertz, we are not allowed to be recorded. I’m still trying to get a supervisor.

Owen: What your corporate policy says and what is legal where I am physically calling from are two different matters. We still have a contract around the rental of this car. Did the person on the prior call tell you the car was drivable? Is that what you’re reporting?

Patty: If you’re still recording the call, I will not respond. Bear with me, I’m getting a supervisor.

Owen: You are refusing to answer the question. You said you’re recording the call at the beginning of the call.

Patty: All right, I am so sorry for the hold. There is going to be a supervisor calling you. His name is Alex.

Owen: I need you to clarify what you said before. I need to understand.

Patty: If we are still being recorded, I will not reply.

Owen: I want to say something important for you to hear. I need your name.

Patty: My name is Patty.

Owen: Patty, what is your last name?

Patty: We do not give out last names.

Owen: What is your employee identification number?

Patty: We do not have employee numbers.

Owen: I’m going to be subpoenaing these records. You tried to send me out on the road in an undrivable car based on what you reported was a drivable car.

Patty: I did not say that one time. I am making that very clear.

Owen: That is why I’m going to subpoena this call. You tried to send me out in a car —

Patty: You go right ahead and do that. I am telling you right now. I did not tell you to drive the car.

[prior to the recording, that is exactly what her colleague said, on their recorded line.

Keep in mind, my kid is in the backseat and we are still waiting for the cops, who will let me know the suspect was apprehended].

Patty: You said you wanted it towed. I told you what was said prior was not put in the notes. When you requested the tow, I said I would tow it.

Owen: So when I subpoena that prior call and this call, are they going to say different things, Patty?

Patty: As far as I know, no sir.

Owen: Because you would understand that if those things are different, that would be fraudulent.

Patty: We will disconnect due to you recording the call. A supervisor will be calling you back.

Owen: In what timeframe will the supervisor be calling me back?

Patty: Once we hang up he should be calling you.

Owen: I look forward to it.

[Patty the unidentifiable Hertz Employee got me her manager on the phone]

lex: Hi, my name is Alex. I’m the available supervisor here at emergency roadside. Before we continue, I do have to advise that calls cannot be recorded on your end. They are already recorded on our end, so we’ll have to ask you to stop recording.

Owen: Why do you have the right to do that?

Alex: Because that’s our policy, sir.

Owen: Your corporate policy and the legality here in the state of Connecticut are different. Are you aware of that?

Alex: I’m aware that the calls are already being recorded and I’m going to need you to start the call.

Recording ended.

[I relent, they tow the car…the legal back and forth is still going].

Traffic accidents are both avoidable and lead to the kinds of interactions that are usually the province of certain healthcare companies. Exhausting! Now, on to the public health facts…

The scope of dangerous human drivers is worth noting.

In 2024, there were 107 deaths in the US per day. That was a grand total of 39,254 deaths in America that year, or 1.19 per 1 million miles traveled.

Also in 2024, there were more than 6.18 million crashes across the United States. This was a slight increase from prior years, as fatal crashes declined. That works out to roughly 16,800 police-reported crashes per day, about 700 per hour, and nearly 12 every minute.

Of those, 11,904 were killed by people who had been alcohol impaired—that is 30% of all crashes. The number of opportunities for more death a destruction from drunk driving is vastly higher: 15.5 million American are estimated to have chosen to drink and drive in 2023, and there were 804,926 people were arrested for suspected DUI in 2024, representing 11% of all arrests nationwide.

We can all agree AI, like your author, for all its flaws, doesn’t have an unquenchable thirst for alcohol. For those who missed the memo, Owen Muir, your author, doesn’t drink. I have already laid the crime of rape (and it’s culturally sanctioned nature) firmly at the hands (overwhelmingly) of both men and alcohol. We can’t yet automate men away entirely, but what if we could replace drunk drivers with robots?

We can.

Waymo has been self-driving for 170m miles.

Swiss Re, one of the world’s leading reinsurers, analyzed 25 million Waymo miles and concluded Waymo produced 92% fewer bodily injury claims and 88% fewer property damage claims than human-driven vehicles.

That is 0.01176 fatalities per 1m miles traveled caused by Waymo’s robot driver, versus 1.19 for humans. That is 101.1904x safer.

Tesla's track record is not as good when it comes it's grandly named “full self driving”…

Their own internal data, which only reports when there is a crash that triggers an air bag, demonstrates that it's still safer than human drivers.

Tesla’s Q1 2025 safety report shows Autopilot users drove 7.44 million miles before a crash, compared to 1.51 million miles for non-Autopilot Tesla drivers — roughly 9x safer than the U.S. national average by Tesla’s own calculation

Now, I'm tempted to take Tesla's data with a grain of salt, but let's just say it's true.

It's something like nine times safer than humans driving Teslas. Even if we divide that in half, it's still better than humans. That's more living beautiful, brilliant younger sisters with an engineering degrees still with us, and less time spending talking to lawyers at car insurance companies.

Humans, I think it's safe to say, are terrible drivers. This is not obvious immediately to everyone. One of the people to whom it wasn't obvious is my daughter. I did an interview with Quinn, in a diner, about two weeks after our accident. I'm gonna let her— with her child like wonder and strangely prescient wisdom—take us out.

Owen: We’re doing an interview for the newsletter. What’s your name?

Quinn: Quinn.

Owen: What are your feelings on self-driving cars?

Quinn: Well, first of all, they can be helpful, but there should be limits on it. They’re very dangerous.

Owen: Why do you think they’re dangerous?

Quinn: Because the AI could miscommunicate.

Owen: How dangerous do you think humans are at driving cars?

Quinn: Humans driving cars? It’s safer than an AI model.

Owen: What if I told you that’s not true? Waymo has driven millions of miles and is 100 times less likely to crash than a human driver. What would you say?

Quinn: I would say it’s definitely a lot safer, but it’s also about what you trust.

Owen: Why does trust matter? It’s either safer or it’s not safer.

Quinn: Because trust is what you put on the car. If you’re really nervous, you could grab the—

Owen: Let’s say you’re in the back seat of a car driving itself. Would you rather AI drive the car or daddy drive the car?

Quinn: AI. You’re terrible at driving, Daddy. No offense.

Owen: So if you have the choice between AI and Daddy, you’re choosing AI?

Quinn: Yeah. I’d rather we both be in the back seat and have AI drive.

Owen: So why do you think other people think it’s dangerous — including you at the beginning of this interview?

Quinn: Because people don’t trust it. The AI could mess up.

Owen: Sure, but humans mess up all the time. There are tens of thousands of fatalities every year. We were actually in a car accident with a drunk driver. Do you think AI would be a better driver than that drunk driver?

Quinn: Yes.

Owen: What if AI got rid of all drunk drivers?

Quinn: That’s impossible.

Owen: Why?

Quinn: Because... oh. If no humans were driving, no one could drive drunk.

Owen: There are about 40,000 people in the U.S. who die every year from traffic accidents. Would you rather have AI drive everything or humans drive everything?

Quinn: AI.

Owen: Is that the opposite of what you said in the beginning?

Quinn: Yeah, because I was thinking of Tesla. My experience with the Tesla wasn’t good. It was messing up. It could only stay in a straight line.

Owen: How about the Rivian when I had AI driving?

Quinn: That was mid. It could also only drive in a straight line. But if it could drive around the city like Waymo can, I would trust it more. If the Rivian had better self-driving like Waymo, then I would actually trust it.

Owen: So if people could trust it and it was proven safer, they’d like it?

Quinn: Yes, but some people would still be against it. Like with the American Revolution — not everyone agreed. There were loyalists and patriots. The patriots would be the people who support self-driving, and the loyalists would be the people who are against it. Some people are loyal to the old ways no matter what.

Owen: And in the beginning of this interview, you thought AI was dangerous because you’d only ever been in a Tesla?

Quinn: Yeah, and it was horrible. But then you changed my mind when you gave me the data about Waymo’s safety record. I didn’t know the brand name, but I’ve actually been in a Waymo in San Francisco. That was the one!

Owen: Thank you, Quinn.

There you have it, from my wonderful daughter, it's not just about safety, it's about trust.

Subscribe now

In loving memory of Kaitlynn Fisher. Katie, you were Magic, and if there's any justice in this universe, we'll get to laugh about it all together on the other side someday.
